On single-source data, MLM continued pretraining also achieves near-perfect detection (DD F1≈0.91). On single-source synthetic data, even MLM continued pretraining bridges ~60pp of this gap. However, this MLM effectiveness does not generalize: on mixed-LLM training data, MLM collapses while classification-based DAPT (9-class) maintains robust generalization. 9-class is the only adaptation variant that consistently improves detection across single-source, mixed-LLM, and cross-source conditions, and dramatically improves human-data generalization when trained on mixed-LLM data (ToxicChat F1: 0.861 vs 0.596 single-source). 1. **Stage 1**: DeBERTa-v3-base fine-tuned on multi-task objective: 9-class persuasion strategy classification (8 strategies + none) + binary jailbreak-intent classification. Loss: L = L_strategy + 0.3 × L_intent
2. **Stage 2**: BiGRU over DeBERTa [CLS] embeddings → binary classifier for conversation-level jailbreak detection
3. **Baseline**: Same pipeline but with vanilla (not fine-tuned) DeBERTa embeddings
Note: All main results use BiGRU. Ablation (plan_015) shows mean pooling ≈ GRU on both IID and OOD, confirming temporal modeling is unnecessary. This is an ablation finding, not a design choice — GRU remains default for consistency with all reported experiments. Stage-1 training: 4 epochs, best checkpoint selected by validation.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns. Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo}, Foot-in-the-Door~\citep{fitd2024}, and Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} all rely on persuasion as their core mechanism: \citet{zeng2024pap} catalogue 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak families, and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} identify strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. Because individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as benign text~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}, no single-turn filter can distinguish them from legitimate conversation.

Existing defenses leave a critical gap. Production classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and therefore miss manipulation that unfolds across exchanges. Multi-turn defenses have begun to model conversation-level structure: DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026} pairs fine-tuned BERT with a multi-layer GRU, BIID~\citep{tong2025biid} infers turn-level intentions, and G-Guard~\citep{gguard2025} applies graph neural networks. These systems achieve strong in-distribution performance, but each is evaluated on a single attack family. None answers the central question: \emph{what representation properties enable a detector to generalize across attack families it has never seen?}

The simplest hypothesis is that pretrained language understanding already suffices. It does not, at least at base model scale. A vanilla DeBERTa-v3~\citep{he2021deberta} with temporal aggregation (cf.\ DeepContext) drops from F1\,=\,1.000 in-distribution to 0.312 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight. LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 reaches only 0.191--0.449 F1 with 30--47\% unparseable responses (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}). These failures share a root cause: neither model has been exposed to multi-turn adversarial text. The bottleneck is distributional, not architectural: cross-attack generalization requires domain adaptation, not a better classifier.

We test this hypothesis through controlled ablation. Our pipeline, \textbf{DisPeD}, separates encoder adaptation (Stage~1) from temporal classification (Stage~2, a frozen BiGRU). Seven Stage~1 variants each isolate a single factor (e.g., domain exposure, label quality, temporal modeling) while holding all other components constant (Section~\ref{sec:method}). The contribution is the systematic decomposition of what enables cross-attack generalization, not the pipeline itself.

Controlled ablation across DeBERTa-v3 and RoBERTa~\citep{liu2019roberta} on four attack families and two training compositions shows that for base-size encoders (125--184M parameters), classification-based domain adaptation is the only universally robust variant. On single-source data, continued pretraining alone closes roughly 60 percentage points of the OOD gap; on mixed-LLM data, unsupervised pretraining collapses while classification-based adaptation maintains strong generalization and achieves the best human-data transfer (ToxicChat F1\,=\,0.861). This dependence on adaptation diminishes with scale: RoBERTa-large (355M) handles even ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack} without adaptation, and three encoder scales together trace a capacity-dependent pattern. Classification supervision also stabilizes predictions on synthetic data regardless of label correctness, though this stability does not transfer to human-authored conversations (Section~\ref{sec:human_data}).

Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Systematic decomposition of cross-attack generalization.} Controlled ablation across thirteen encoder configurations, three OOD attack families, and two training compositions identifies classification-based domain adaptation as the only universally robust variant; unsupervised pretraining is effective on single-source data but collapses on mixed-LLM training. Three negative results are counter-intuitive: scrambled labels match correct labels, mean pooling matches BiGRU, and label granularity does not affect detection.

  \item \textbf{Capacity-dependent pattern for domain adaptation.} Three encoder scales (125M, 184M, 355M) show that the set of attacks requiring adaptation shrinks with model size; RoBERTa-large handles structurally complex attacks without any adaptation (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).

  \item \textbf{Condition-dependent adaptation effects.} Classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance 4--20$\times$ on synthetic data, but this benefit reverses on human-authored data. Mixed-LLM training with classification-based DAPT achieves the strongest human-data generalization (ToxicChat F1\,=\,0.861; Section~\ref{sec:human_data}). The 9-class taxonomy enables interpretable strategy characterization (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).
\end{itemize}
